# Summary: Choosing a Method {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: setup-summary
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")
```

## Which Method? A Flowchart {.unnumbered}

Every problem in this book answers the same three questions:

1. **Which parameter?** A mean, a proportion or a variance.
2. **How many groups?** One, two, or three or more.
3. **What is special about the data?** Is $\sigma$ known? Are the samples paired?
   Are the variances equal? Are there blocks?

```{r}
#| label: fig-flowchart
#| fig-cap: "Choosing a method. Numbers in brackets are the sections."
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-width: 7.5
leaf <- data.frame(y = 11:1, label = c(
  "σ known: z test (2.1)", "σ unknown: t test (2.2)",
  "Paired: paired t test (3.4)", "Independent, equal variances: pooled t (3.6)",
  "Independent, unequal variances: Welch t (3.6)",
  "No blocks: one-way ANOVA, CRD (4.1)", "Blocks: ANOVA, RCBD (4.3)",
  "z test for p (2.3)", "z test for p1 − p2 (3.1)",
  "Chi-square test for σ² (2.4)", "F test for σ1²/σ2² (3.5)"))
grp <- data.frame(label = c("One group", "Two groups", "Three or more", "One group",
                            "Two groups", "One group", "Two groups"),
                  y = c(10.5, 8, 5.5, 4, 3, 2, 1))
grp_leaves <- list(c(11, 10), c(9, 8, 7), c(6, 5), 4, 3, 2, 1)
par_ <- data.frame(label = c("Mean", "Proportion", "Variance"), y = c(8, 3.5, 1.5))
par_groups <- list(1:3, 4:5, 6:7)
xs <- c(0, 1.5, 3.1)
seg <- data.frame()
for (i in 1:3) for (j in par_groups[[i]])
  seg <- rbind(seg, data.frame(x = xs[1] + 0.45, xend = xs[2] - 0.6, y = par_$y[i], yend = grp$y[j]))
for (j in 1:7) for (l in grp_leaves[[j]])
  seg <- rbind(seg, data.frame(x = xs[2] + 0.6, xend = xs[3] - 0.05, y = grp$y[j], yend = l))
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = seg, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_label(data = par_, aes(xs[1], y, label = label), fontface = "bold", size = 3.6, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_label(data = grp, aes(xs[2], y, label = label), size = 3.3) +
  geom_label(data = leaf, aes(xs[3], y, label = label), hjust = 0, size = 3.2, fill = "#eef4fb") +
  annotate("text", x = xs[3], y = 0.2, hjust = 0, size = 3, fontface = "italic",
           label = "After ANOVA rejects H0: Tukey (4.2)") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.5, 6.4)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 11.5)) +
  theme_void()
```

| Method | Test statistic | Distribution | R |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Mean, $\sigma$ known | $z = \dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ | $z$ | -- |
| Mean, $\sigma$ unknown | $t = \dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}$ | $t$, $n-1$ | `t.test(x, mu = )` |
| Proportion | $z = \dfrac{\hat{p}-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}$ | $z$ | -- |
| Variance | $\chi^2 = \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}$ | $\chi^2$, $n-1$ | -- |
| Two proportions | $z = \dfrac{\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}$ | $z$ | -- |
| Paired means | $t = \dfrac{\bar{d}}{s_d/\sqrt{n}}$ | $t$, $n-1$ | `t.test(x1, x2, paired = TRUE)` |
| Two variances | $F = s_1^2/s_2^2$ | $F$, $(n_1-1, n_2-1)$ | `var.test(x1, x2)` |
| Two means, pooled | $t = \dfrac{\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{s_p^2(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}$ | $t$, $n_1+n_2-2$ | `t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = TRUE)` |
| Two means, Welch | -- | $t$ | `t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE)` |
| ANOVA (CRD) | $F = \text{MSTr}/\text{MSE}$ | $F$, $(k-1, N-k)$ | `summary(aov(y ~ trt))` |
| ANOVA (RCBD) | $F = \text{MSTr}/\text{MSE}$ | $F$, $(t-1, (t-1)(b-1))$ | `summary(aov(y ~ trt + block))` |
| Tukey | -- | -- | `TukeyHSD(model)` |

## Which Method? Practice {.unnumbered}

For each study, name the parameter(s), the method and the section.

(a) The Bank of Thailand wants to know whether the share of households with
credit-card debt has risen above 35%.
(b) A researcher compares the mean wage of 40 workers in Chiang Mai with the
mean wage of 35 workers in Khon Kaen.
(c) The same 25 firms report their profits before and after a tax change.
(d) An analyst asks whether the daily returns of a stock index have become more
volatile than a standard deviation of 1.2%.
(e) Four fertilizer subsidy schemes are each tried in five districts, with the
scheme randomly assigned to villages within each district.
(f) A survey compares the proportion of men and of women who own a business.

::: {.answer title="Which Method? Practice"}
(a) One proportion, $z$ test for $p$ (2.3), $H_1: p > 0.35$.

(b) Two independent means: $F$ test for the variances first, then pooled or Welch $t$ (3.5, 3.6).

(c) Paired means: paired $t$ test on the differences (3.4).

(d) One variance: chi-square test, $H_1: \sigma^2 > 1.44$ (2.4).

(e) Four means with blocks (districts): RCBD ANOVA (4.3), then Tukey if $H_0$ is rejected.

(f) Two proportions: $z$ test for $p_1 - p_2$ (3.1).
:::

```{r}
#| label: mixed
m2 <- list(n1 = 9, x1 = 52.4, s1 = 6.1, n2 = 13, x2 = 47.8, s2 = 5.4)
m2$v1 <- round(m2$s1^2, 4); m2$v2 <- round(m2$s2^2, 4)
m2$F <- round(m2$v1 / m2$v2, 3)
m2$Fhi <- crit_F(.975, 8, 12); m2$Flo <- crit_F(.025, 8, 12)
m2$sp2 <- round((8 * m2$v1 + 12 * m2$v2) / 20, 4)
m2$se <- round(sqrt(m2$sp2 * (1 / 9 + 1 / 13)), 4)
m2$t <- round((m2$x1 - m2$x2) / m2$se, 3); m2$tc <- crit_t(.975, 20)

m3_chi <- round(14 * 0.8^2 / 1, 3); m3_c <- crit_chisq(.05, 14)

set.seed(2771)
bill_before <- round(rnorm(8, 2400, 450), -1)
bill_after <- bill_before - round(rnorm(8, 380, 260), -1)
m4 <- t.test(bill_after, bill_before, paired = TRUE, alternative = "less")

set.seed(2772)
ads <- data.frame(channel = factor(rep(c("TV", "Online", "Radio", "Print"), each = 5),
                                   levels = c("TV", "Online", "Radio", "Print")),
                  sales = round(c(rnorm(5, 52, 4), rnorm(5, 58, 4), rnorm(5, 47, 4), rnorm(5, 46, 4)), 1))
model_ads <- aov(sales ~ channel, data = ads)
m5 <- summary(model_ads)[[1]]
m5t <- TukeyHSD(model_ads)$channel

m6 <- list(n = 20, xbar = 3.42, s = 0.58)
m6$se <- round(m6$s / sqrt(m6$n), 4); m6$tc <- crit_t(.975, 19); m6$me <- m6$tc * m6$se
```

## Mixed Problems {.unnumbered}

Use $\alpha$ = 0.05 and the five steps.

### M1 {.unnumbered}

In a survey of 500 workers, 210 have a second job. Test whether more
than 40% of workers have a second job. Use the critical region.

::: {.workspace lines="12"}
:::

::: {.answer title="M1"}
One proportion (2.3). $\hat{p} = 210/500 = 0.42$.

**Step 1.** $H_0: p = 0.40 \quad H_1: p > 0.40$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $\sqrt{0.40(0.60)/500} = `r num(round(sqrt(.24/500), 4))`$;
$z_{\text{cal}} = (0.42 - 0.40)/`r num(round(sqrt(.24/500), 4))` = `r fmt(round(0.02/round(sqrt(.24/500), 4), 3), 3)`$

**Step 4.** Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$.

**Step 5.** $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(round(0.02/round(sqrt(.24/500), 4), 3), 3)`$ does not fall in the
critical region ($`r fmt(round(0.02/round(sqrt(.24/500), 4), 3), 3)` < `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$), so we
accept $H_0$. That is, the proportion of workers with a second job is equal to
0.40 at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::

### M2 {.unnumbered}

The monthly profit (thousand baht) of `r m2$n1` cafés in the old city has
$\bar{x}$ = `r m2$x1`, $s$ = `r m2$s1`; that of `r m2$n2` cafés near the
university has $\bar{x}$ = `r m2$x2`, $s$ = `r m2$s2`. (a) Use the $F$ test with the
critical region to check the variances. (b) Test whether the mean profits are
different, using the critical region.

::: {.workspace lines="16"}
:::

::: {.answer title="M2"}
**(a)** $H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$ vs $H_1: \sigma_1^2 \ne \sigma_2^2$.
$F_{\text{cal}} = `r num(m2$v1)`/`r num(m2$v2)` = `r fmt(m2$F, 3)`$, df = (8, 12).
Critical region: $F_{\text{cal}} < 1/F_{0.975,\,12,\,8} = `r num(m2$Flo)`$ or
$F_{\text{cal}} > F_{0.975,\,8,\,12} = `r m2$Fhi`$. $F_{\text{cal}}$ does not fall
in the critical region, so we accept $H_0$: the variances are equal. Use the pooled $t$ test.

**(b)**

**Step 1.** $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 \quad H_1: \mu_1 \ne \mu_2$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $s_p^2 = [8(`r num(m2$v1)`) + 12(`r num(m2$v2)`)]/20 = `r num(m2$sp2)`$;
SE $= \sqrt{`r num(m2$sp2)`(1/9 + 1/13)} = `r num(m2$se)`$;
$t_{\text{cal}} = (`r m2$x1` - `r m2$x2`)/`r num(m2$se)` = `r fmt(m2$t, 3)`$, df = 20

**Step 4.** Critical region: $t_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-m2$tc, 3)`$ or $t_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(m2$tc, 3)`$.

**Step 5.** $t_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(m2$t, 3)`$ does not fall in the critical region
($`r fmt(-m2$tc, 3)` < `r fmt(m2$t, 3)` < `r fmt(m2$tc, 3)`$), so we accept $H_0$.
That is, the mean monthly profits of cafés in the two areas are equal at the
0.05 level of significance.
:::

### M3 {.unnumbered}

A central bank wants the standard deviation of the monthly inflation rate
to be less than 1 percentage point. Over 15 months, $s$ = 0.8. Assume normality
and test whether the target is met, using the critical region.

::: {.workspace lines="12"}
:::

::: {.answer title="M3"}
One variance (2.4).

**Step 1.** $H_0: \sigma^2 = 1 \quad H_1: \sigma^2 < 1$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = 14(0.64)/1 = `r fmt(m3_chi, 3)`$, df = 14

**Step 4.** $\chi^2_{0.05,\,14} = `r m3_c`$. Critical region: $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < `r m3_c`$.

**Step 5.** $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(m3_chi, 3)`$ does not fall in the critical region
($`r fmt(m3_chi, 3)` > `r m3_c`$), so we accept $H_0$. That is, the standard
deviation of monthly inflation is equal to 1 percentage point at the 0.05 level
of significance; the data do not show that the target is met.
:::

### M4 {.unnumbered}

Eight households installed solar panels. Their monthly electricity
bills (baht) before and after installation were recorded. Did the mean bill
decrease?

```{r}
#| label: r-data-m4
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(vec_code("bill_before", bill_before), vec_code("bill_after", bill_after))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-m4
#| echo: !expr show_code
t.test(bill_after, bill_before, paired = TRUE, alternative = "less")
```

::: {.workspace lines="10"}
:::

::: {.answer title="M4"}
Paired means (3.4), $d$ = after $-$ before.

**Step 1.** $H_0: \mu_d = 0 \quad H_1: \mu_d < 0$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $t_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(m4$statistic, 3)`$, df = `r m4$parameter`

**Step 4.** p-value = `r fmt(m4$p.value, 4)`

**Step 5.** p-value = `r fmt(m4$p.value, 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$.
That is, the mean monthly electricity bill decreased after installing solar
panels at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::

### M5 {.unnumbered}

Twenty stores are randomly assigned to four advertising channels (TV,
Online, Radio, Print), five stores each, and weekly sales are recorded.
(a) Test whether mean sales differ among the channels. (b) If they do, which
channels differ?

```{r}
#| label: r-data-m5
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(grp_code("channel", levels(ads$channel), each = 5), vec_code("sales", ads$sales))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-m5
#| echo: !expr show_code
model_ads <- aov(sales ~ channel)
summary(model_ads)
TukeyHSD(model_ads)
```

::: {.workspace lines="14"}
:::

::: {.answer title="M5"}
**(a)** One-way ANOVA, CRD (4.1).

**Step 1.** $H_0: \mu_{TV} = \mu_{O} = \mu_{R} = \mu_{P} \quad H_1:$ at least one mean is different

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $F_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(m5[1, "F value"], 3)`$, df = (`r m5[1, "Df"]`, `r m5[2, "Df"]`)

**Step 4.** p-value = `r fmt(m5[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)`

**Step 5.** p-value = `r fmt(m5[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject
$H_0$. That is, mean weekly sales are not all equal across the four channels at
the 0.05 level of significance.

**(b)** Pairs with p adj < 0.05: `r paste(gsub("-", " $-$ ", rownames(m5t)[m5t[, "p adj"] < 0.05]), collapse = ", ")`.
TV and Online have equal mean sales, Radio and Print have equal mean sales, and
both TV and Online have higher mean sales than both Radio and Print.
:::

### M6 {.unnumbered}

The mean household size in a district is estimated from 20 households:
$\bar{x}$ = `r m6$xbar`, $s$ = `r m6$s`. Construct a 95% confidence interval for
the mean household size.

::: {.workspace lines="6"}
:::

::: {.answer title="M6"}
One mean, $\sigma$ unknown (2.2). $t_{0.975,\,19} = `r fmt(m6$tc, 3)`$,
$s/\sqrt{n} = `r num(m6$se)`$; $`r m6$xbar` \pm `r fmt(m6$tc, 3)`(`r num(m6$se)`) = `r m6$xbar` \pm `r num(m6$me)`$.
We are 95% confident that the mean household size is between
`r fmt(m6$xbar - m6$me, 2)` and `r fmt(m6$xbar + m6$me, 2)` persons.
:::

## Writing a Full Conclusion {.unnumbered}

A full conclusion has a **decision** and an **interpretation** in the words of
the problem:

> **Decision.** [statistic or p-value] ... so we [reject / accept] $H_0$.
> **Interpretation.** That is, ... at the 0.05 level of significance.

Checklist:

- If you reject $H_0$, write $H_1$ as a sentence; if you accept $H_0$, write $H_0$ as a sentence.
- Name the population and the variable (not just "the mean").
- For a two-sided test that rejects $H_0$, add the direction from the sample statistics.
- For ANOVA, "not all equal"; then use Tukey to say which ones differ.

Write the decision and the interpretation for each result.

(a) $H_0: \mu = 15000$, $H_1: \mu \ne 15000$ for the mean monthly rent (baht) in a
district; $t_{\text{cal}} = -2.514$, critical region $|t_{\text{cal}}| > 2.064$, $\bar{x}$ = 13,850.
(b) $H_0: p_1 = p_2$, $H_1: p_1 > p_2$ for the proportions of urban (1) and rural (2)
households using mobile banking; p-value = 0.0832.
(c) One-way ANOVA comparing mean loan sizes at three types of lender; p-value = 0.0007.

::: {.workspace lines="12"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Writing a Full Conclusion"}
(a) $t_{\text{cal}} = -2.514$ falls in the critical region ($-2.514 < -2.064$),
so we reject $H_0$. That is, the mean monthly rent in the district is different
from 15,000 baht at the 0.05 level of significance; since $\bar{x}$ = 13,850, it is
lower than 15,000 baht.

(b) p-value = 0.0832 $\ge$ $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we accept $H_0$. That is, the
proportions of urban and rural households using mobile banking are equal at the
0.05 level of significance.

(c) p-value = 0.0007 < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is, the mean loan
sizes are not all equal across the three types of lender at the 0.05 level of
significance. (Use Tukey's method to find which types differ.)
:::

::: {.solutions-here level="2"}
:::
